segments.text: Good afternoon. I'm the guy they put right after lunch to make sure everybody wakes up, I guess. But I hope you had a good lunch and it's a pleasure to be here and be part of this wonderful conference.

I'm learning a lot and also making a lot of contacts here. Africa's energy transition is really, and you've seen that a lot repeated in the videos, about how we drive structural change in our economies to create wealth, industrialize, create jobs and of course power our social services.Dr. Lassina Zerbo this morning made a comment which is very relevant here and I think that's the purpose of this conference.

He said, if countries are not at the table then they are on the menu. And for those of us who are on the continent dealing with energy issues and minerals, we know everybody is trying to get a piece of the African real estate for our minerals, particularly rare earth minerals. There's really a deliberate, what should I call it, struggle to get their hands on as much of those minerals to power the rest of the global energy transition.

Dr. Lassina is right. Either we are engaged in the conversations and prepare ourselves to take advantage of the new wave or yes, we just become part of the menu and just bystanders observing this new revolution. So this conference really is about looking ahead five years from now, six years from now when SMRs or MMRs become cost competitive, will Africa be ready? Country readiness but also regional readiness.
I think that's the purpose here. It's not as if tomorrow morning African countries are immediately going to invest in SMRs or MMRs. The cost is pretty high.

But will we be ready in five or six years? And why is this relevant? I served on the board of Rocky Mountain Institute for a while and they do all kinds of projections on energy transitions and climate change. And last year we had a session where different scholars were showing evidence how very wrong we all were about the solar revolution. All the estimates we made about how fast solar will be deployed were off the mark by 50%.

The revolution moved faster than the analysts had said, meaning industry, technology moved faster, prices went down and yes, countries deployed solar very fast. Is it possible? And I guess that's the question for our panel and for you. Is it possible that in five years, in 10 years, SMRs and MMRs might even prove the analysts wrong, that the cost will be driven down and it will become affordable for us? So this conference is about looking ahead and so I want to thank President Kagame and the nuclear agency here for helping us look beyond the horizon and look at possibilities.

For me it's about possibilities. So what is the demand profile like? Africa's energy demand is expected to grow rapidly from 2030 to 2035. our Infrastructure Development Authority, estimates that Africa would need 650 gigawatts of electricity installed from the current base of 260 gigawatts by 2035.
So moving from 260 to 650. And then they project further that by 2040, it will be 700 gigawatts needed. So the demand case is there for more power generation.

To achieve universal access, which is still our challenge, Sustainable Development Goal number seven, we need to connect 80 million Africans every year to electricity, moving from an average of 20 to 23 million per year we're doing now. Again, a quantum leap is needed. All of this in the next decade.

This is why we embrace Mission 300, that has taken all of these issues into consideration and over 30 African countries now have a Mission 300 compass. So my first message here is, work is already ongoing on the planning we need to ensure that Africa is electrified and in fact, we're on a pathway to universal access to energy over the next five to 10 years. We have to take advantage of that if we want to move into nuclear.
We don't have to reinvent the wheel. Mission 300 has all the necessary pillars on policy reforms, energy trade, utility reforms, all packed in. And of course, the resources required.

So we have a base to start from. So what's the financing that is needed? The International Energy Agency estimates that financing needs will grow from the current 2.5 billion per year to about 15 billion per year from now till 2035, if we want to achieve universal access.

A lot of money is needed just to do the basics with the technologies we know. You add on top of that now, the opportunity we see with nuclear, but again, the cost. From what the scientists tell us, an SMR right now, based on all the experiments ongoing, might be $5 billion for three to 400 megawatts.

An MMR, maybe much less, that can produce one megawatt all the way to 50 megawatts, but also very pricey. And therefore, all of that will be driven into tariffs. And for those of us who have served as ministers of energy, we know the headache in our country is about tariffs.
So the pricing of the MMRs and SMRs will be an issue. But perhaps, as I said, we could be very surprised that in fact the cost will be driven down faster. So again, it's about readiness.

How do we get our countries ready, or our regions ready to take advantage of this new renaissance of nuclear technology? So I wanna leave you with five thoughts for the panel to consider. I believe with the cost structures that I see now with SMRs, that the regional approach will be critical. I don't see smaller countries being able to deploy $5 billion to generate three to 400 megawatts to use domestically.

Industrialization is not happening that fast in our countries. So a more regional, sub-regional approach makes sense to me, that you can place an SMR in a country and then the country can trade. Again, pillar two of the Mission 300 has outlined for each country what we need to do more in terms of energy trade, the infrastructure and the interconnections we need to make that happen.

So I believe a regional approach will make sense. President Kagame hinted on that today when he talked about cooperation and avoiding fragmentation. But he begs the question then, regional readiness versus country readiness.

To be ready in a sub-region, a lot of negotiations, the need for harmonizing regulatory frameworks and also other approaches so that there's a common understanding amongst countries. But I really believe the opportunity that exists for MMRs and SMRs will be regional energy trade. That's the base.

But then you ask, how do you finance a plant in Ghana that will supply the rest of West Africa? Why did I choose Ghana? Ghana got their first experimental nuclear facility at the same time as India, in the late 1950s. India, of course, is a nuclear power. We're still learning.

So there's an opportunity here that some countries may be ready, not all, but they can do energy trade. So I believe one issue that the panel should look at are the opportunities for regional trade and harmonization of regulatory frameworks so that we look at how energy trade can be enhanced by deploying these SMRs, but also to make them more cost effective. I have said again that we take advantage of Mission 300

The two colleagues on the panel from the World Bank and African Development Bank have been working with our countries, getting our compacts and our vision documents ready and cost . We know how much we need. And again here, why do I keep emphasizing Mission 300? I was in the development space for a long time with the UN, leading sustainable energy for all and the United Nations Industrial Development Organization.

I worry that when you have a new wave or paradigm coming in, we forget the past. There is still unfinished business of achieving sustainable development goal number seven. So Mission 300 has to be the basis of looking at the possibility of taking advantage of this new nuclear renaissance.
Natural resource-backed financing. I wanted to talk about that. Because again, $5 billion for one SMR, it's quite a bit of money.

So I'm asking myself, what should I tell my president? I'm also an advisor to the president. I say, hey, we've seen this great opportunity. He's also had conversations with the International Energy Agency.
So he's wondering what I'm gonna go back and tell him. Say, well, please say it's $5 billion . Our demand here in Sierra Leone right now is 300 megawatts.

But the mines need another 500. How do we get money to invest in one? We supply the mines and maybe trade with Guinea and Liberia, with whom we have an interconnection. So is it resource-based financing? How do we structure a deal that if it is regional, that all the countries agree on their contribution? Because the plant will supply everybody.
How do we structure that conversation going forward from here? That is going to be a key issue that I think the panel should also consider. But I see possibility and I see hope. I see a lot of hope.

I watched a video the last couple of days preparing to come here of a discussion between the IFC, our brother at the IFC, Mokhtar Diop and Aliko Dangote. In those days when I was leading Sustainable Energy for All, we did events here with Aliko and Tony Blair and others under the leadership of President Kagame. But Aliko said something a couple of weeks ago that really struck me.

He explained how he got $20 billion to build his refinery. But here's the other two things he said. He said, now I want to be the largest producer of urea and possibly fertilizer in the world because I already have the refinery already, the largest in the world.

And of course you know Africa needs a lot of fertilizer too and the rest of the world too. But then he said this, because I'm not sure of the power situation, I want to do 20,000 megawatts of power. Well, that's ambition.

And that's where our minds have to be. There are private sector individuals in some African countries that could potentially be able to raise such capital to be able to deploy these technologies. Not today, but maybe in five years.

If Dangote wants to do 20,000 megawatts because he needs it for his refinery and of course the rest of Nigeria needs it, who knows, he might choose to leapfrog and go into this technology. I use that case study to make the following case. One, we need anchor demand in some locations if we're going to deploy this.

Either the mines or a big operation like Dangote. This could make SMRs probably easier and quicker to deploy than if we just go with governments. Second, I make that case because we sometimes need to look inwards.

We have some capital in our countries that we're not mobilizing enough of that can leverage additional financing from other partners. But Aliko also said, if you're not ready to invest in your continent, nobody else would. And that's what is driving his passion to do these big mega projects.
So I see possibilities, I see possibilities here, but not for now, probably in five years. We have to be ready to ride that wave. Africa, we've missed other waves.

The industrialization wave, the digital wave, we're almost missing as well because of lack of power and other governance and security issues. But can this be one we ride? So I want to thank President Kagame for challenging us to think ahead. And of course, my brother, Lassina.
Lassina and I spent a long time in Vienna. He was CEO of one agency. I was CEO of the Industrial Development Organization.

So these are conversations we've had and he's always pushing us to look beyond the horizon. I hope that you look beyond the horizon and look at possibilities that we don't want to be on the menu. In fact, we want to set the menu and prepare the dinner and the conversations over dinner.
Thank you very much.
I am Yohannes G.Hailu from the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa. I just want to take a moment and highlight what we have heard so far in a few bullets.

From the speech of the excellencies and their suggestions, we have heard fragmentation is something to be avoided. We are all moving in the same direction in this agenda. And there are sufficient cases for us to consider how we can solve problems, how to bring effectively nuclear into our energy system, and how to make it investable.

We have also heard the case that we cannot talk about transformation, industrialization, competitiveness, if we cannot address the fundamental issue of reliable baseload. And that is where the nuclear conversation is coming in. We are also reminded that of all the other regions in the world, if you compare us, Africa is the most dynamic continent.

Four in five, one in four population by 2050 would be residing in Africa. If you look at our economic growth, we will require four times as much power by 2040 than we are consuming today. That is a radical transformation in the next 20 years that we're anticipating.

To what extent the energy sector will respond? How effectively will we respond? How do we finance it? Which technologies are going to be our ally? These are all questions that are being asked, and nuclear has just entered the conversation. I thank Dr. Yumkella for identifying potential breakthroughs in terms of how we can pull this together. Regionalism, resource-backed financing, and anchored demand in industry are highlighted.

In the next conversation, we are going to talk about scale and how we can make nuclear power investable in Africa. To do so, we are privileged to be joined for this conversation by a distinguished economist, former minister of finance and economic planning of the Republic of Rwanda, the servants former president of the African Development Bank, the chair of the Global Fund for Health Initiatives, as well as AU special envoy on financing. Please join me in warmly welcoming Dr. Donald Kaberuka for the conversation.

To start our conversation, distinguished participants, we heard phenomenal news this morning that Rwanda has transitioned from phase one preparation, hard work, into phase two. So we all join in congratulating Rwanda for this particular success. What this means is now phase two questions will surface.

Phase one, why do we need a nuclear? Is that the case for nuclear? How do we integrate nuclear energy into our energy mix? A lot of these issues would have to be answered. Do we have institutions, regulatory systems, and laws? Now to the second phase, difficult questions, either investment case for nuclear, Dr. Kaberuka, you have extensive experience at national, continental, and global level in terms of capital. Is there a sufficient case, investment case, for nuclear power development today in Africa? Thank you.
Dr Donald Kaberuka
Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for coming to Rwanda, but I'm sure the minister will be doing that officially. I want to step back a bit and just tell you a number.

By the way, I want to correct two things I had this morning. The World Bank and African Development Bank were not the ones who were refusing to do nuclear. It is the shareholders of those institutions.

It was the owners of those institutions. So I want to make sure that you are fair and we say what is happening. Now, even when the World Bank or the FDB tries to do a large-scale non-nuclear project, it takes a long time because of a lot of the ESG requirements for the projects.

So this is an issue for shareholders of those institutions. I'm saying this because it's okay that they sign on to nuclear, but I hope that now they don't impose such a long list of institutions that will go back to square one. In your country, Ethiopia has just commissioned a 6,000 megawatt hydropower on the Renaissance Dam.
That is the biggest hydropower in Africa. It is almost three times the size of the Aswan Dam in Egypt. They did not borrow money from international institutions.

Some of us helped a bit with transmission lines, but they mobilized money internally and many other sources which we can discuss because that was the case. But another number I want to share with you. India is 10% of Africa's size.

10%, I think, roughly. The total installed capacity of power in India is about 560 gigawatts of electricity, I think. The whole of Africa, from north to south, total installed capacity is half that of India, 30% of which is renewable, I think.
But even then, the two-thirds of this 254 gigawatts is mainly in North Africa and Southern Africa. It shows you how far we have to go. India is 10% of Africa's size.
But there is a difference. It is one country. We are 54 fragmented countries.

Hence, the importance of what my president was saying about fragmentation. Some of these things have to be done at scale. One more thing I wanted to say to you, but Kande, where are you? I think Kande should have been here being interviewed, not me.

Thank you for making a correction which I really hope people here don't misunderstand. This morning, when I was talking about small reactors, micro-reactors, people thought they were cheap. No, no, no, no.

So to give you a rough idea, a megawatt of electricity, if it is a hydro, and it is not very complicated with civil works, people being expropriated, roughly it would be about a million dollars, at least when I was in the ADB. I don't know now. Maybe it has gone up or down.
About a million dollars, roughly, per megawatt. Now Kande said it is 1. Yeah. You see the numbers? They are quite small in macro, but they have quite a lot of capital.
So I hope we don't get confused. One last point, because I want to step back a bit, is on this regional cooperation. We all desire regional cooperation.

It is an important aspiration. But who in this room has not heard about INGA being able to produce 50,000 megawatts of electricity? Many of us have tried to do that project. Before me, after me, when I was in the bank, all kinds of formulas have been tried.
Now, it is not a technical problem that we can't put turbines in the river. It is not a demand problem. There is so much demand around 50,000 megawatts.

It is impossible to put in place a structure which saves the location where the hydro is and the water market. So I end by saying that one of the beauties of nuclear power is that it is not location-specific. Hydro is location-specific.
Look, take the whole of West Africa. Many of those rivers emanate from the highlands of Guinea. So it is location-specific, including Indonesia.

Okay. If you look at hydro in Africa, many of the sources are in the Guinea highlands, in the Congo basin, Ethiopian highlands, I think the Zambezi basin, and then highlands of Lesotho. Okay, so it's location-specific.
So is solar, so is wind. But nuclear is not location-specific. And so that is one of its main attractions.
But then there's other issues we can discuss. Thank you for that insight. Now, that takes us to the issue of finance.

Dr. Yohannes already talked about how even for massive projects, there are cases where Africa has mobilized resources to make them happen. The case of Ethiopia. And he mentioned challenges around the Grand Inga.

And in terms of financeability, bankability, the issue about geographic flexibility of nuclear technology and peculiarities, that can be advantages. But the fact remains, even though private sector participation in energy infrastructure development has been growing in Africa, reaching around 25, 26 percent, almost a quarter now. However, in the global context, we still capture a fraction of that resource to come into the continent.
Globally, there's good news. Global capital is growing. More than three trillion, the last number we checked.

However, not even three percent of long-term capital is coming to Africa. So in your view and your global experience around these issues, what do you think are the critical barriers that are blocking this global capital to come and connect to these kinds of solutions? I'll come to that in a moment.
But let me say also that in my long experience of funding energy projects, of all types, I always found that at the heart of it were what I call the three A's. Energy may be there. It is available.

But is it accessible? Second A, is it affordable? And many governments struggle a lot with access and affordability. And so we end up with systems of tariffs, which meet the social need purpose, but which undermine the capacity of the national off-takers and their balance sheet. I don't know why this would cause a problem, but you are there to defend free speech, no? You see, our colleagues in Southern Africa, in South Africa, they acknowledge this is not a problem.

They had one of the cheapest powers, I think, at the beginning was around five cents per kilowatt hour. But then as the economy was expanding, demand was increasing. All right? They accumulated a huge amount of commercial losses because the national off-taker, ESCOM, wasn't able to invest upstream for the increased demand.

I could tell you dozens of many other countries where social policy, what should be the tariffs, and economic logic come into conflict. And so the national off-takers, the balance sheet is so weak, you cannot, from a basis, even for IPPs. Now, my successor at the African Development Bank has come up with a concept he calls the new African architecture.
Is there somebody from FDB here? Maybe there must be. Please talk about that. And he's building on the initiative of many institutions, financial institutions, of which you are one.
They have put in place something called the Alliance of African Financial Institutions. Okay. What is the idea? Here we have African financial institutions.

They have different mandates and missions. Some do project finance, other trade finance, others guarantees, others insurance, others re-insurance. So they're trying to come together in this financial architecture.

And the idea is, before we talk about external capital, let's talk about our own capital. But institutional investors in Africa, whether pension funds, insurance companies, whatever it is, have requirements before they provide you with their money. It is not their money.
So I think what I like about this new architecture, it looks as internally what you can mobilize a trillion dollars. Okay. Although a large part of it is South Africa.
And then we can then work with foreign capital. Now, this is totally feasible. But it requires a lot of work.

And I want to say this to you. Professor Samuel DAMPARE, he was at Kennedy School, he's no longer there now, had observed something which is extremely interesting. That in the global North, what is called the global North, the aging part of the world, because of those demographics, savings have increased dramatically.
And outside the domain of technology, the returns are quite not as interesting as they could be. Now, those parts of the world are aging all the time. So savings will increase.

From Singapore, Taiwan, China, to most of Europe, Russia, US is a bit. Now, so you have got aging population, increased savings, a lot of savings. On this side, in the global South, it is opposite problem.

Dynamic demographics, negative savings. Who is going to do the work of intermediating the need for return by the capital in the North and the needs for investment by the demography in the South? That is why I think that beyond what my successor, the FDB is trying to do, the new African financial architecture, we need also a global financial architecture to do that job of ensuring that capital can get a good return where there is demography, not as charity, but as self-interest. Now, if we do that, we could finance many things, even beyond nuclear, even beyond nuclear, because the needs of this continent are quite big.

But I think there has to be a way of saying to institutional investors in the North, look, we have our own capital here, Fort William, but explain to me how we can go to Scandinavian institutional investors and say, we Africans are investing in US paper, in other European asset classes, because we think our continent is risky. But now we're asking to come and take the risk. Does that make sense? There has to be sequencing.
And if we do that, I think we can get the work done. It won't happen in a day, but it will happen. Thank you very much.

I know we have run out of time for this session, but there's one burning question, and I hope Dr. Kaberuka would answer it very briefly. You have financed a lot of infrastructure projects during your tenure at the African Development Bank. You have dealt with a lot of infrastructure issues nationally and globally.

As we embark into first of a kind nuclear development in the continent, new systems, new plans coming, you have seen how infrastructure projects succeed. You might have also come across situations where you might have been briefed. This or that project, for whatever reason or assumption around it, didn't work, it failed.

What are the lessons that need to be transferred one or two very quickly that we can learn and benefit from prior continental infrastructure projects that we cannot repeat and make these nuclear projects quite successful? However, there's something specific about nuclear projects. I'm speaking under the control of Kande. I think this issue of regulation, so that you can build trust in terms of safety, waste management, what they call it, back-end cost.

Back-end cost is a jargon for when this reactor has done its time and you have to decommission it, there's still some costs along the way. So that regulatory space and its independence is extremely important. Now, in many countries in Africa, where the national off-taker is solid, I'm talking about electricity.
You can talk about highways if you want. And there's an independent regulator who decides on tariffs. Things have worked very well.
Kenya is a very good example. Tunisia is another good example. Ghana for some time was a very good example as well.
But in many other countries it has been a challenge. So I think it's a combination of balancing social policy and economic logic. It is an issue of independence, not just in the text, in fact.

So that tariffs can be set at a rate which gives a return to the investors. Because many of these nuclear plants are simply done by IPPs. They'll be signing long-term agreements with the national off-takers or maybe mining companies and all this.
There has to be someone who independently can set up the tariffs. Thank you very much. There were a lot of questions to raise and a lot of insights to be shared.
But that's all the time we have. Please join me in sincerely appreciating the insights and contributions of Dr. Kaberuka . Thank you very much
To join the panel, Mr. Erik Fernstrom, Regional Director for Infrastructure, Eastern and Southern Africa of the World Bank. Please join us in the panel. Please welcome Mr. Eric.

Also to join the panel, Ms. Lucy Chege , Associate Executive, Project and Infrastructure Finance Department, the Trade and Development Bank Group. Welcome to the panel. Also joining the panel is Mr. Kevin Kariuki, Vice President for Power, Energy, Climate, and Green Growth of the African Development Bank.
You're welcome to the panel, sir. So continuing the conversation, distinguished panelists, welcome to this panel to continue the conversation. We do have 20 minutes in this particular discussion.

Again, a lot of insights to be shared, a lot of items to be discussed, but we'll try our level best to deliver all of that within the time given to us. Now, we have heard, two insightful inputs from Dr. Kaberuka, Dr. Yumkella, on the importance of restoring bankability, on the importance of restoring economic viability within our electricity system, the issue of avoiding fragmentation in regionalism, all of that to improve the bankability and the investability of nuclear projects in the continent. Now, from your perspective, what is the most pressing challenge that we need to address in terms of accelerating the investability aspect of nuclear projects in the continent? Let me start from my immediate neighbor here, and then we'll take it from there.

Thank you. First of all, I think the previous two speakers have made it really easy to start this panel because I think they really highlighted the system aspects of what we're discussing here today. And I think it starts with the reliability, the affordability, and the availability of power in countries and in regions.

So almost 40 of the sub-Saharan utilities are below break-even. Some are even bankrupt, right? This is not a good base to build a long-term development trajectory. So we need to treat the energy sector, the national utilities, and the revenue balance in our sector as importantly as we deal with the phases in the Atomic Energy Agency's development phases, right? Because the two need to go together.

If they are delinked, there will not be a power plant financed. Thank you for that. But I think a key message that is coming out is that nuclear energy, even though we might have distinct legal text, distinct regulatory institutions, nonetheless is part and parcel of the energy market, the electricity market.

Therefore, critical issues around tariff, around utilities, around creditworthiness, around infrastructure readiness would also apply to the system. I think it's very important to integrate those two. Thank you.

Ms. Chege, for your input on the same question. Thank you. So I would also add, I mean, there's been a lot that has been said, but I could also add that one of the missing links in the system, really, we don't have long-term funding sufficient for it within the continent.

And without that, there's no way to deliver on these long-term projects. Because if you look at the sort of funding that would be needed to address the type of numbers that was spoken about in the previous discussion, you're going to need long-term funding. And we really don't have sufficient long-term funding for that to happen.

So I think that's one of the other areas that has not been discussed yet. And thank you for that input. Mr. Kariuki, from your perspective from the bank, what do you see as a critical barrier or a critical element that needs to be addressed in the context of investability of nuclear energy in Africa? Thank you very much, Johannes.

I think for me, the undoubtedly weakest link is the lack of demand aggregation. And why I say this is because this is what will inform the sources of energy and therefore technology and the capacity additions, as well as retirements that are required. And when I say this, if you look at, for example, if you are going to be worried about demand in two to three years, the only logical technology is solar.

If you're talking about three to five years, you're looking at wind and gas. If you're looking at five to 10 years, you're looking at hydro or geothermal. But if, and if you have the time, if you're looking at 15 years, then nuclear becomes a viable technology.

And I want to cite an example of a real life situation on the continent. Currently, South Africa is discussing its what we call the 2025 integrated resource plan. And here it is saying that in the year 2039, they will have to be meeting a demand of about 105 megawatts.

And of that 105 megawatts, 16 megawatts, sorry, not megawatts, gigawatts, one or five gigawatts. Of that, 16 gigawatts will be from gas to power, 5.2 gigawatts of nuclear, in addition to 25 gigawatts of solar and 34 gigawatts of wind, as well as 8.5 gigawatts of battery energy storage. So you need to look at the planning horizon if it is 25 years, and look at what technology will serve the interconnected grid best at a particular time.

Thank you. Thank you for that contribution. I think the suggestions and discussions so far taking us in the direction of systems thinking, long-term planning, careful integration of technology on the basis of costing as their analysis and putting the right pieces together.

Earlier from Dr. Kaberuka, we heard about the tension in the sector between socially oriented policies to deliver social good, at the same time restoring economic viability of the sector, which requires making sure the economic fundamentals within our electricity markets are right. And this will continue to inflict implications on energy, on any energy technology, but the same would be the case for nuclear. And now, Mr. Fernstrom, if I come to you from prior experience with multilateral development banks, it is not just about the project.
The project has to be designed well. It has to be bankable. It has to have the right configuration that would make it attractive and de-risked to be financed.

But that project is also sitting within the context of an electricity market that would have its own characteristics, which is already sitting within the context of the national macroeconomic conditions, business environment, perhaps beyond the scope of the energy sector itself. So in this sense, from an MDB perspective, what would you have to see in a project in this cascading layer of considerations that would make it possible? But within that context, I think we are warned that Dr. Kaberuka also said that if we make this process exceedingly difficult with a list of requirements, even if the position is to finance nuclear energy, the process might kill it. So balancing these two, how do you say what are the key elements that need to be satisfied for this kind of project to be appealing to MDBs? Well, thank you.

And first, I think Dr. Kaberuka mentioned INGA, and I have 250 million deployed today on maybe the world's hardest to build hydro project. So we are not risk averse, but I think we need to respect the process where we together address some of these issues to actually make it viable and buildable in a way, right? So just starting on the non-nuclear side, I think for those of you that haven't looked at the compact that Dr. Yumkella mentioned, please look into them. We now currently have 30 mission 300 compacts that have been developed by our partner countries laying out exactly what is needed in terms of reforms, in terms of power market integration, in terms of investment and private sector regulation, …, to actually make this power market viable and vibrant, right? So that's a very important part and we are putting a substantial amount of money, but also a massive amount of thinking with our partners, AFDB and TDB as well across the region on this.

Now on the nuclear side, what we need to see is a very methodical development of all the aspects of safety, security, regulation and the fit of the candidate for the generation, right? And in that respect, the nuclear power plant behaves just like any other baseload. It has to be placed. You cannot shut it on and off all the time, right? So you have to have a sufficient demand pool in your country to actually make this project viable.

So as was mentioned earlier today, we have partnered with the International Atomic Energy Agency very closely in supporting the phased approach of nuclear development. So we will, together with the portfolio of energy financing we have deployed in many of the countries that are present here today, as well as new resources we are raising with partners to support the technical assistance, we can go along with that journey. And then, you know, we will together determine when both the cost, the viability and the readiness sort of intersect and when we can come to an investment decision, right? But, you know, we are not there yet in many of these cases but I think we will get there.
And when I listened to some of the discussion, I had the great privilege of living here in Kigali 2007 today . The supply in Rwanda, if I remember correctly, was 30 megawatts. Today is 300.

It's a factor of 10 times. So these are countries that evolve and I don't think we should be stuck on a status quo. We should look at the African market as an exponentially growing market, very exciting market where in the future, much larger power needs and much larger placement of loads will be possible.

Thank you. Indeed, indeed. We are in a very dynamic, not only energy sector but in terms of democracy economy, one of the most dynamic regions in the world and we need not to get stuck on not necessarily legacy policies but innovation, policy, regulatory, market, financial innovation should be part and parcel of that process.

I think that fits very well into the theme of this particular summit as well. Ms. chege , from a lender perspective from Trade and Development Bank Group, in terms of going beyond ambition to transaction, what do you need to see in proposed nuclear projects to assess its bankability? Thank you so much for the question. I think one of the issues Dr. Kaberuka has already spoken about is clarity in the regulatory environment that is in the planning.

It needs to be clear how the program fits into the overall country's energy mix and planning. So I think that's one, just to make sure that this coherence of policy and the reason why that's important from a lender perspective because these are long-term investments. So you want to be sure that the direction that you're going strategically is the one that is aligned with the government.

The second thing I wanted to speak about is about government support. And I'm going to draw lessons here from some of the work that I was doing previously with the IPP program, which was in South Africa which was very successful in terms of raising both local and international investments. And one of the key pillars of that program was really the government support.

And the reason why this is important for a lender is that the government has to support the lenders with various provisions. If there's termination of contracts, the lenders need to know that the government is behind that and will support the program. The second thing about government support is really to also support the utility.

I think we've heard about the utilities and the issues that they're faced with. And really it's important that the government stands behind those utilities, because as a lender, if most of these transactions will be done through an IPP program, as was alluded to by Dr. Kaberuka, you need to be sure that the government is supporting that utility. And the support can take various forms.

I think each country has its own method, so to speak. So I wouldn't prescribe that one country has its own, each country has its own way of dealing with the government support. But from a lender perspective, you want to be sure that if there's a problem, the government is standing behind the utility and also the program.

Now, there are many other issues. I won't talk through all of them, because I think the idea is to make sure that there's a bankable project. But one of the key things is about capacity and the capacity of the contracting entities.

So we know that this is a long-term process. And I think we heard maybe we're getting ready for a program that is five years from now. But it's important that there's capability of the contractors, because one of the things that can stall any process is having contractors and contracting parties that are not able to deliver, because that will bring downfall of the whole program and ensure that it doesn't succeed.
So that's another area that I think is very important. Contracting parties, we need to be sure and need to look at their strength. I think I can just stop there.

There are other issues, but I think those are the main ones that we'd want to consider. Indeed, there are many, many more issues that are the time that was given to us, but I appreciate that contribution. Now, we do have five minutes, and I'm going to go to Mr. Kariuki.

I would like to add one additional element as we'll conclude on the same issue of bankability, especially we talked about the industrial component, the productive use component, the reliable off-tech component being critical for project economics related to nuclear. So what kind of scale of investment are we talking about? And how do we see nuclear power playing a fundamental role in terms of strengthening industrialization, competitiveness, and all those transformative aspirations that they have? Now, related to that, in terms of closing, what role do you see African Development Bank playing in the entire value chain of support for nuclear energy from pre-feasibility studies, feasibility assessments, early project support, potentially de-risking in some form of capital mobilization to later states? How do you see FDB playing a role in this articulated aspiration of African member states? Thank you very much, Ioannis. I think the first part of the question, the International Energy Agency projects a scenario in which Africa's overall energy demand will double by 2040, with electricity demand also expected to double by 2050, relative to 2025 levels, in terms of energy to about 2,300 terawatt hours.

And in terms of megawatts, you had Dr. Yumkella and Dr. Kaberuka talked about 254 to 600 megawatts, but this will grow to about 600, 700 megawatts. And this is of course driven by rapid industrialization, urbanization, as well as the fastest growing population globally. And in terms of investments, you're looking at $100 billion per year.

But in terms of the role of nuclear energy here, I would say that, and this is purely my uninformed guess, based on the current state of readiness of the Africa nuclear energy sector. Of course, the long lead times, I think IAEA will tell you that a nuclear program will result in a power plant that will take about 15 years. The long lead times, and of course the development of technology such as SMRs, and we've also had MMRs.

I expect that nuclear energy will start contributing significantly into the energy sector towards the year 2040. And in my view, my personal view, it could reach about 5% by 2050. Because if you look at it today, only Egypt's 4.8 gigawatt El Daba power plant that is due for commissioning into 2028, 2029, and you have South Africa's proposed 5,200 megawatts expected in 2039, are the only significant additions to Africa's and only, sorry, South Africa's and only Africa nuclear power plant in the 1.86 gigawatt at Kobak.

And in terms of what the bank can do and to support, here I want to say very unequivocally, we are very keen to support what Lucy also alluded to, the development of long-term released cost power expansion plans for countries. I can say without fear of contradiction that I'm sure the World Bank, between the World Bank and us, will be able to finance this because these are very, very integral. Because at the end of the day, we are not developing power plants purely for the sake of it.

We also want affordable power. So these are the plans that will inform the capacity additions that you require, what you need to retire, as well as the duty. Mr. Kariuki, in 30 seconds, we are running out of time.
Okay. Please summarize. I'm summarizing.

So we will be happy to support countries develop long-term credible power expansion plans. And I think that if we do that, we will be creating a good basis for any energy mix, including renewable energy and of course, nuclear energy. Let me stop there.

Thank you very much. Ms. Chege, from the perspective of the Trade and Development Bank Group, in one minute, for countries that are looking for, who are our partners, who are our allies, in terms of supporting part of the value chain towards development of these nuclear projects, what can your institution offer to be a partner and to be a valuable part of that process for member states? Thank you again for the question. From the Trade and Development Bank side, we'd also be keen to be part of the process and to assist our member states in terms of the planning and getting towards the vision that is desired.

It might need doing some work in terms of the planning of the overall energy mix. And we are willing to support those processes and work towards the solution that is required for the continent. Thank you.

Thank you very much. And Mr. Fernstrom, in the final input for this particular panel session, the announcement of the World Bank has created a lot of excitement, and has generated a lot of enthusiasm around it. So I will not ask you what the World Bank will do.

I will ask you what more will the World Bank do to support member states? So I think that, I mean, there are two things here. One is we have been out of this kind of forum for decades, if ever, right? So we have a lot of, we're very humble. We have a lot of learning to do in nuclear space.

And me being here is part of my learning journey and the institutional learning journey to engage more with project developers, with countries, with regulators and with agencies, right? So we are doing a lot of that and this is a ramp up phase. So hopefully next year, when we meet again, we will have more to talk about in terms of what we do internally to strengthen our capacity to engage, right? On the concrete stuff, I think we are already, and I hope I don't promise too much now, but I believe we will have our first investments in the nuclear power space within this calendar year. These are sort of brownfield or what we call renovation projects, but it shows an engagement that the institution has in this space across the globe.

And we have to recognize that there are many, many different types of investment cases that we need to look at. Everything from the mining side of nuclear and uranium to existing nuclear power countries that need revamping, repowering, et cetera, to these cases of new developments that we see in this continent. Thank you.

Exciting, a lot of support, a lot of positive outlook and desire to engage with countries as they embark on this direction. We are also excited about the technology for small countries like my own. I'm originally from Eritrea, or for large countries like Nigeria, the possibilities are there.
That's all the time we have, ladies and gentlemen. Please join me in appreciating the insights and contributions of this distinguished panel. Thank you very much.

parts.title: Liu Jing, China Atomic Energy Authority

segments.text: First of all, I would like to express my warmest congratulations on behalf of the National Institute of Nuclear Energy to the public for hosting this session. I also listened attentively to the wonderful speeches I would also like to share some of my experiences with you. First of all, small-scale and micro-scale projects are certainly more expensive.

They are definitely more expensive than our large-scale commercialized nuclear power plants. However, their total cost is low. This is more suitable for small-scale and micro-scale projects in areas where our power grid is small and we want to have nuclear power development.

I think that small-scale and micro-scale projects still have a certain development prospect. The small-scale projects we usually refer to are projects that require less than 300 megawatts of power. The micro-scale projects we refer to are projects that require less than 10 megawatts of power.

Secondly, the introduction of a nuclear power development or the construction of a reactor is definitely not a matter of a power plant or a device. As the experts mentioned earlier, it is a construction of a supervision system. At the same time, it is also a matter of the entire community's consideration.

Whether it is the disposal of nuclear waste and radioactive waste or the disposal of recycled waste, it is a matter of the entire community's consideration in this country and in this region. It is a matter of the entire community's consideration. It is a matter of the entire community's consideration.

Thirdly, in the early stages of development, the support of the government is of paramount importance. The development of nuclear power depends entirely on the commercialization and the financing of the market, especially the construction of nuclear power plants. From China's experience, there is still a certain degree of difficulty.
The early stages of investment and the establishment of the system require the support of the government. I am willing to share my thoughts with the experts and officials I have just heard. I

First, what is the current situation? What stage are we at now? Second, what kind of work have we done for the development of nuclear power development, or the application of nuclear technology, what kind of work have we done, Thirdly, in the future, we plan to, or we want to do something for the development of Africa's energy, especially nuclear energy and technology. First, let me talk about China's current nuclear energy development.

So far, China has built 61 nuclear power plants, 51 nuclear power plants, and 112 nuclear power plants. All of them are 1,000 megawatts, or 1,000 megawatts, of nuclear power plants. So we will also put 51 nuclear power plants into operation 30 years from now.
In total, by 2030, our total number of nuclear power plants will be the world's largest. The world's first commercial power plant, Linglong No. 1, is about to be put into operation.

12.5 million, or 125 megawatts, of Linglong power plants will be able to produce electricity this year. At the same time, we have advanced technologies such as high-temperature gas-cooled power plants and land-based flammable power plants. We already have the technology for generating electricity.

We have also built the world's most complete nuclear power industry chain, from the supply of nuclear fuels to the design and construction of reactors, to engineering, construction, adjustment, operation, and safety supervision. We have realized the self-control of the whole chain, and we have been able to fully satisfy all the equipment we manufacture in China. At the same time, we can support more than 40 base-building engineering capabilities.

In addition, in the field of nuclear technology application, we will apply nuclear technology to agricultural production, industrial upgrading, medical health, climate governance, and deep integration, so that nuclear technology can truly serve the people and improve the environment. We have achieved considerable results. This is our current development situation.

On the other hand, I would like to introduce some of the things we have done for some African countries. Since the 1980s, China has helped Algeria to build the Berlin Nuclear Research Center, built a satellite reactor for Ghana and Nigeria, and completed a low-agriculture upgrade, and laid the foundation for the development of nuclear technology in these countries and regions. We exported six steam generators to South Africa's Copenhagen nuclear power plant, and donated Gamma-Daw tumor treatment equipment to Morocco.

At the same time, since the launch of the Chinese government's nuclear scholarship project in 2017, we have trained 148 nuclear specialists for 20 African countries. In the field of nuclear medicine, China has organized a training program for radiotherapy physicists from African countries, and trained 38 radiotherapy physicists for 22 African countries. In recent years, we have continued to deepen cooperation with Rwanda, Kenya, Sudan, and other countries, and share the technical experience of small-scale modular reactors.

At the same time, we have met the needs of the people in the fields of nuclear medicine, and we also want to help the high-quality development of the African economy and society through Chinese nuclear technology. As for the future, I would like to make four suggestions. First, we need to increase clean energy investment to help Africa's energy independence.

China has formed a complete nuclear power production chain and sufficient technical verification capacity, which can help Africa greatly reduce the risk of first-class construction. We support African countries to develop nuclear power according to their own needs, and we are willing to discuss the use of multi-factor financing windows, mixed financing and export new generation, and other diversified tools, to provide planning design, investment financing, engineering construction, transport and maintenance, talent cultivation, and a whole solution. We focus on small-scale modular reactor power plants, nuclear-capable power grids, and other investment contributions.

Second, we need to deepen technological innovation cooperation and cultivate self-development capacity. China will open a national-level nuclear research platform training base and build a nuclear-capable joint laboratory and technical research center in Africa. We will send expert teams to Africa for technical guidance, and we will jointly develop technological innovation cooperation.

Third, we need to expand the application of the civil-industry field, and we will expand the application of renewable African industrial upgrades. China will introduce nuclear technology into the African economy, promote radiation-preventing, food-preservative technology, help improve food production, and ensure food security. We will promote the application of nuclear technology in industrial testing, material modification, environmental management, and other areas, and help Africa's industrial system improve and transform.

We will build a nuclear medical center, provide renewable drugs, tumor treatment equipment, and technical support, and make active contributions to Africa's early implementation of the 2030 UN Sustainable Development Goals. Fourth, we need to strengthen the construction of nuclear safety capabilities, and work together to ensure safety barriers. China is willing to strengthen the dialogue on nuclear safety, nuclear security, and emergency policy, supervise experience exchanges, and assist Africa in establishing a strong nuclear safety, nuclear security, and legal system, supervision mechanism, and emergency response system.

At the same time, I also invite all the guests to attend the China-Africa Peace Use Nuclear Technology Forum to discuss the grand plan for the development of nuclear energy, and the prospects of nuclear energy cooperation, and to work tirelessly to realize the vision of a nuclear-free home.
